summary: BBN discusses connecting a host to an IMP over a long distance, beyond about 2000 feet and possibly tens of miles. Any good solution should have an extremely low undetected error rate, not be limited to low bandwidth, and let the host open multiple network conversations.

plainLanguage.summary: Usually a computer sits right next to its network box. This note asks how to connect them across a long distance without losing data.

subtitle: Connecting a host computer to the network from a long distance away

tldr.problem: Standard IMP host connections require a short hard-wire connection. Some hosts need to connect via long-distance cables or telephone circuits, requiring a new interface design.
tldr.mechanism: Full-duplex transmission uses the Binary Synchronous format with a 24-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC) for error detection, retransmission software on both the IMP and host sides, and special formatting hardware at each end.
tldr.outcome: A complete specification for long-distance host-to-IMP connections that maintains reliability and bandwidth without sacrificing the host's ability to open multiple network conversations.

today: This RFC describes a preliminary design for long-distance host connections to the ARPA Network. It is a historical document on early network infrastructure design, predating modern distance-independent networking protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 263 addresses the problem of connecting a host computer to an IMP over long-distance connections, beyond about 2,000 feet and potentially tens of miles. The normal connection is a short hard-wire link, but long-distance connections—whether via dedicated cables or telephone circuits—require a different design to maintain reliability and performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Network computers usually sit next to their network box. This RFC asks how to connect them from far away.

sections.title: Design Criteria
sections.content: Any solution must satisfy three key criteria. First, the connection must have an extremely low undetected error rate to maintain data integrity over distance. Second, bandwidth should not be intrinsically limited to a low value, preserving the host's ability to send useful amounts of data. Third, the connection must allow the host to establish multiple network conversations with all the capabilities of a normal short-distance connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The long-distance connection must not lose data, must be fast enough, and must let the computer do everything a normal connection can do.

sections.title: The Technical Approach
sections.content: The design uses full-duplex transmission with Binary Synchronous format, the same format used for inter-IMP communication. The IMP end uses a hardware interface similar to its standard 50-kilobit modem interface, which frames outgoing data blocks with special characters and appends a 24-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC). The host must provide matching formatting, de-formatting and checking facilities. Both the IMP and host receive retransmission software implementing positive acknowledgment and timeout techniques for reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection sends data in both directions at once, uses error-checking codes on each chunk, and resends anything that gets lost.

sections.title: Implementation and Specification
sections.content: The host must provide a software or hardware front-end to its NCP that generates CRCs, tests for CRC errors, and provides retransmission logic. This front-end may be implemented in host software, special-purpose hardware, a minicomputer, or any other method the host organization finds suitable. Detailed specifications will be documented once the design is complete, likely as an update to BBN report number 1822. BBN is open to discussing this interface with interested organizations, though detailed design specifications were not yet finalized at the time of this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host will need its own code or hardware to handle error checking and resending. BBN will publish full instructions later.

references.text: McKenzie, A., "Connecting Computers to MLC Ports", RFC 241.
